source.title: Demystifying Small Language Models for Edge Deployment
source.authors: Zhen-Yan Lu; Xiang Li; Dong-Qi Cai; Rongjie Yi; Fang-Ming Liu; Wei Liu; Jian Luan; Xiwen Zhang; N. Lane; Mengwei Xu

page_placements.theme: Data quality, relevance and selection change scaling efficiency

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted figure text in Appendix B is garbled, but the relevant ablation table and its accompanying discussion are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests architecture-related loss differences using a controlled training ablation, but it does not reproduce the original scaling-law sweeps or held-out-loss measurement.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Chinchilla and compares reported training-token counts and calculated training costs, but does not measure held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, or compute, fit scaling curves, or search for loss-minimising allocations at fixed compute. Its broad downstream benchmark results are not fitted or used to test downstream predictability. The relevant architecture ablation reports final training loss; a separate data-quality comparison reports downstream accuracy.
record.test_reason: Appendix G.1 trains 18 models of about 100M parameters on the same 20B tokens. It varies depth (3–33 layers), width, activation and attention heads, and reports final loss. This is a controlled check, by a different method, of whether shape matters at fixed parameter count (V4). Nothing else in the paper fits or tests scaling curves.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that architecture has a negligible effect on final training loss but strongly affects inference speed (up to 5.22× in decoding). They also conclude that data quality outweighs quantity, and that SLMs are heavily over-trained relative to Chinchilla.
record.recipe_differences: This is an architecture ablation at similar model sizes, not a scaling-law sweep; it reports final training loss rather than held-out loss and does not fit power laws or optimize a fixed-compute allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture configuration varies across the 18 ablation models; the study reports final training-loss values across those variants.

fits_no_version.finding: Two same-architecture 500M models: DCLM data with 100B tokens reaches 0.52 average accuracy; RefinedWeb+StarCoder with 200B tokens reaches 0.47.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-data quality can outweigh doubling training tokens for downstream accuracy at fixed model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers), 2025
record.problems: The architecture ablation uses similar rather than identical parameter counts, reports training rather than held-out loss, and provides no uncertainty estimates for the relevant losses.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant ablation results left out. The paper's reported training-token counts, calculated training costs, runtime measurements, and general benchmark results were not entered as scaling-law rows because they do not measure held-out loss scaling or a fixed-compute loss optimum.

untested.parts: Held-out (rather than training) loss; parameter counts above about 100M; feed-forward ratio and aspect ratio separated from depth; seed variance. The parameter counts are not exactly matched (99.5–106.7M).
Not tested: no loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
Not tested: only notes that SLMs are trained far beyond the Chinchilla 20:1 ratio.
Not tested in a controlled way: only uncontrolled cross-model correlations (Fig. 3b).

missing.what: Cross-model correlation between training tokens and average downstream accuracy. The paper calls it positive but weak, mainly below 700B tokens, and says data quality dominates above 1T. It covers heterogeneous public SLMs with no controls, so it is context for V6, not a test.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's main body is an edge-deployment benchmark of public SLMs. The only scaling-relevant result is the Table 9 ablation. Per-row states for r1–r18 are only meaningful jointly. No uncertainty or seeds are reported. The loss is training loss, but held-out loss on a single-epoch 20B-token run is likely similar.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or held-out pretraining-loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions evaluated against larger runs.
Token counts and estimated training costs are discussed, but no fixed-compute loss-minimising parameter/token allocation is tested.
The architecture ablation measures final training loss, not held-out loss; parameter counts are similar but not identical.
No other modality or training regime is tested for the same power-law form.
The study reports downstream benchmark performance but does not test whether it is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits are compared across setup or fitting choices, and no loss curves are tested for bending.

rows.operation_detail: Trained an architecture variant on the same dataset and 20B tokens as the other ablation models.
rows.note: The paper describes the 18 models as similar in parameter size and says architecture has a negligible effect on final training loss.
rows.check: A single loss value cannot show an effect alone; the V4 state comes from comparing all 18 rows. This 3-layer, 106.73M model is the largest yet has among the worst losses (3.76). That fits the original finding that very shallow nets deviate, so it is not a contradiction.

relationships.condition: 18 decoder variants of about 100M parameters (3–33 layers, hidden 448–1280, ReLU/SiLU, 4 or 16 heads), 20B tokens, final training loss
relationships.reason: Losses span only 3.58–3.81 (r1–r18); the authors call the effect negligible. The largest gaps come from the 3-layer extremes (r1, r2) and fewer heads (r12, r15), each about 0.1–0.2. The measure is training loss, one run each.
relationships.display_finding: Final training losses ranged from 3.58 to 3.81, with the largest gaps of about 0.1–0.2 associated with three-layer extremes and fewer heads.
